title: Voice Agents: the good, the bad, and the ugly

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 55%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building production voice agents with streaming interaction, transcription challenges, and realtime conversational loops. Multi-agent architecture patterns and LLM-as-judge evaluation methodology are extensively discussed as supporting themes. The voice agent patterns are broadly applicable but demonstrated through an enterprise interview automation use case at Fortune 500 companies. The talk traces the journey from an initial monolithic-prompt prototype through multi-agent development, systematic evaluation, and production deployment at scale. Requires familiarity with LLM APIs, prompt engineering, and basic conversational AI architecture. The talk presents a real-world case study of building and deploying a production AI voice agent with a live demo. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting evidence anchors.

summary: Eddie Seagull, CTO at Fractional AI, presents a case study of an AI voice agent that automates consulting-style research interviews—conducting in-depth qualitative interviews with employees at large companies to understand their workflows. This process traditionally required costly consultants, weeks of scheduling, and significant overhead. The goal was to build an agent that conducts natural conversations (not form-filling), interviews hundreds of people simultaneously, and automatically transcribes responses for downstream data extraction. Seagull first outlines why voice agents are hard: LLM hallucinations, subjective evaluation metrics, latency in conversational UIs, transcription difficulties, and streaming (versus batched) environments all compound existing AI challenges. The team started with OpenAI's real-time API and a monolithic prompt containing all interview questions, but soon needed better navigation. They pivoted to one-question-at-a-time with tool use, letting the LLM signal when to advance. A persistent problem emerged: the LLM rabbit-holed on follow-up questions, reluctant to move on. They introduced a background 'drift detector' agent to monitor the transcript and force progression when needed. Goals and priorities were added as first-class concepts to give the LLM the 'why' behind each question. A 'next question agent' was introduced for non-linear interview flow. A significant transcription challenge emerged: OpenAI's realtime API uses Whisper as a side model for transcription, which produces bizarre outputs from silence or background noise (e.g., 'creeping Dippity Dippity Dippity Dippity'), with no API-level knobs to tune. They added a separate transcript-filtering agent that evaluates conversation context and hides likely transcription errors from the user UI while the core model retains full context. As agents multiplied, complexity made it hard to know which to update and regressions became common. To move beyond 'vibes-driven' iteration, they built an eval suite using LLM-as-judge to measure attributes like clarity, completeness, and professionalism. With no objective ground truth, they introduced synthetic conversations—LLM-faked personas (e.g., a 'snarky teenager' running a Fortune 500 company)—to simulate diverse interviewees and run automated eval at scale. Seagull concludes that simply calling an API with prompt engineering gets you far but is insufficient for robust production; out-of-band text-domain agents, tool use for constraining behavior, and evals are essential even without perfect ground truth.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Voice agents compound existing LLM challenges with transcription errors, streaming environments, and latency sensitivity in conversational UIs.
A monolithic prompt containing all questions doesn't scale; sending one question at a time with tool use enables better navigation and control.
LLMs naturally rabbit-hole on follow-up questions; a background drift detector agent can monitor the transcript and force progression when needed.
Goals and priorities give the LLM context for the 'why' behind each question, improving follow-up quality and rephrasing.

Whisper-based transcription in OpenAI's realtime API produces unpredictable outputs from silence or noise; a separate transcript-filtering agent can hide embarrassing errors from users while preserving core model context.
Adding many side agents creates complexity and regression risk; systematic evaluation is needed to move beyond vibes-driven iteration.
LLM-as-judge eval suites measuring attributes like clarity, completeness, and professionalism provide useful (if imperfect) systematic metrics for voice agent quality.
Synthetic conversations with LLM-faked personas enable automated, scalable testing across diverse user types when no objective ground truth exists.
Calling an API with prompt engineering gets you far but is insufficient for robust production voice apps; out-of-band agents, tool use, and evals are essential.
AI interview agents can replace expensive consulting workflows, conducting hundreds of interviews simultaneously with automatic transcription.

sections.title: Voice Agent Challenges
sections.summary: Seagull introduces why voice agents are especially hard: LLM hallucinations, difficult-to-define evaluation metrics, latency in conversational UIs, transcription challenges, and streaming environments all compound existing AI problems.

sections.title: Case Study: Automating Consulting Interviews
sections.summary: The use case is automating consulting-style research interviews at Fortune 500 companies. Traditional interviews require expensive consultants, scheduling overhead, and weeks of effort. The goal is an AI agent that conducts natural conversations, interviews hundreds simultaneously, and provides automatic transcription.

sections.title: Live Demo
sections.summary: Seagull demonstrates the interview agent with a simple test configuration, showing natural back-and-forth conversation with confirmation of answers and graceful closing.

sections.title: Architecture Evolution: From Monolithic Prompt to Multi-Agent System
sections.summary: The architecture evolved from a monolithic prompt with all questions to a one-question-at-a-time approach with tool use for navigation. A drift detector background agent monitors the transcript to force progression when the LLM rabbit-holes. Goals and priorities were added as first-class concepts to guide rephrasing and follow-ups. A next question agent was introduced to provide non-linear interview flow.

sections.title: Transcription Challenges and Whisper Side Model
sections.summary: OpenAI's realtime API uses Whisper as a side model for transcription while the core model operates in the sound domain. Whisper converts everything to text, producing bizarre outputs from silence or background noise (e.g., 'creeping Dippity Dippity Dippity Dippity'). There are no API-level knobs to tune this behavior.

sections.title: Transcript Filtering Agent
sections.summary: To handle embarrassing transcription errors, a separate agent evaluates the full conversation context and decides whether to hide transcript segments from the user. The core model still receives full context, so it can gracefully re-ask questions when transcription is hidden.

sections.title: Complexity and the Need for Evaluation
sections.summary: As side agents multiply to fix issues piecemeal, complexity makes it unclear which agent to update and regressions are common. Seagull emphasizes the need to move beyond vibes-driven iteration toward systematic, metrics-driven evaluation using LLM-as-judge to measure attributes like clarity, completeness, and professionalism.

sections.title: Synthetic Conversations for Testing
sections.summary: With no objective ground truth, the team introduced synthetic conversations using LLM-faked personas (e.g., a snarky teenager running a Fortune 500 company) to simulate diverse interviewees. The eval suite runs over these synthetic interviews to produce average metrics across expected user populations, enabling automated, scalable testing.

sections.title: Wrap-Up and Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Seagull concludes that simply calling an API with prompt engineering is wishful thinking for robust voice apps. Essential additions include out-of-band text-domain agents for checks, tool use for constraining and instrumenting behavior, and evals to measure and guide development even without objective ground truth.
